ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Participants were presented with sets of six pseudowords and selected the items that elicited the most positive and most negative emotional responses; they subsequently provided a plausible definition for each selected item using an affirmative sentence.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants were presented with sets of six pseudowords and selected the items that elicited the most positive and most negative emotional responses; they subsequently provided a plausible definition for each selected item using an affirmative sentence.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .05", "p < .05", "p < .05"), 
    Text = c("Nine of the ten quality associations were significant at the p < .05 level, with MiniLM-L12 as the exception, and eight of the ten specificity associations were significant, with MiniLM-L12 and MPNet as the exceptions.", 
    "For definition quality, 120 of the 121 correlations were positive, and 102 had p < .05.", 
    "All 110 off-diagonal quality correlations were positive, and 92 were significant with p < .05."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .804", "p = .886"), Sentence = c("Spearman correlations between fastText-predicted iconicity and these new measures were negligible for both definition quality (ρ = .008, p = .804) and specificity (ρ = -.005, p = .886) and were significantly smaller than those obtained using the pseudoword vectors (p < .001).", "Spearman correlations between fastText-predicted iconicity and these new measures were negligible for both definition quality (ρ = .008, p = .804) and specificity (ρ = -.005, p = .886) and were significantly smaller than those obtained using the pseudoword vectors (p < .001)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 158 columns across 16 data files.
#### Issues Identified

8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("brysbaert_2012_SUBTLEX_POS.csv", "check_responses_2.csv", "dingemanse_thompson_2020.csv", "iconicity_ratings_cleaned.csv", "iconicity_ratings_raw.csv", "pseudoint_EXP2_all_newpart.csv", "pseudoword_interpretations_v2.csv", "raw_ratings_full_anonymized_01_12_2022.csv" ), Column = c("All_freqs_SUBTLEX", "response", "nmorph", "word", "word", "response", "interpretation", "word"), Issues = c("#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 93% numeric but 3721 values cannot be parsed: \"993445
🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Values look like personal information: ip_address (233 values, 0%)", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: not sure/NOT SURE
↔️ Whitespace — 13 values with leading/trailing whitespace: \" It means \\\"\"No\\\"\" but...", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 97% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"#\"", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: lily/Lily", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: Lily/lily", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: An object/an object
↔️ Whitespace — 766 values with leading/trailing whitespace: \"A central lighting ap...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: Happiness/happiness
↔️ Whitespace — 619 values with leading/trailing whitespace: \"Honest is the state o...", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: Lily/lily" )), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `../models/` to `../../models/` (in pp_checks.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.
#### Missing inputs
2 input files the code reads are in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 7 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `oed_all.csv`, `concreteness_trial.rda`, `winter_2017_iconicity.csv`, `perry_et_al_2015.csv`, `gpt2-xl_results_nwords.csv`, `gpt2-xl_results_words.csv`, `raw_ratings_full_01_12_2022.csv`.
#### Parsing
1 R file did not parse and cannot be run (see code_check for the errors).
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 17 scripts: 4 ran without error, 10 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 1 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

**`setwd()` in the code**

**3 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("power_analysis.R", "MixedModels.R", 
"confirmatory_analyses.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 1L, 1L), 
    "Path(s) it set" = c("path/to/results", "/your/path/to/results", 
    "/results")), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

3 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. text.text: Iconicity, the perceived resemblance between a word's form and meaning, is systematically related to the semantic organization of familiar vocabulary.
This raises the possibility that iconicity-related regularities also constrain how people interpret unfamiliar words.

We tested this proposal by learning mappings from (sub)lexical representations to large-scale English iconicity ratings and examining whether predicted iconicity for pseudowords was associated with the semantic quality and specificity of human-generated definitions.

Higher iconicity predicted from semantic representations was associated with definitions that aligned more closely with their target pseudowords and distinguished them more selectively from alternative forms.
In contrast, orthographic features predicted iconicity in familiar words but showed no corresponding associations with pseudoword definitions.
The positive associations for semantic representations generalized across multiple encoders, including analyses in which different models were used to predict iconicity and evaluate definitions.
These findings suggest that iconicity-related semantic structure in familiar vocabulary is associated with the construction of meanings for unfamiliar forms.

They are consistent with discriminative and complementary learning accounts in which previously acquired form-meaning relations provide graded constraints on novel interpretations and, more broadly, they connect theories of iconicity grounded in perceptual and experiential resemblance with distributional accounts of lexical knowledge, suggesting that linguistic experience organizes and supports the generalization of resemblance-related semantic information to novel forms.

I recall when my wife told me how, during an official celebration in a village near Pavia, a man named Marièt approached the poorly dressed mayor and asked him in the Pavese dialect, "ghevat no un gram gabænæï da mæt sü?"
(roughly, "Didn't you have a bad gabænæï to put on?").
Although the situation provided clues to its interpretation, its intended meaning was immediately clear.
That is, the unfamiliar form gabænæï itself seemed particularly appropriate for what it was meant to convey.

A word without an established meaning can indeed seem meaningful, (possibly) because people draw on patterns already present in familiar vocabulary, including contextual cues (e.g., Snefjella et al., 2020) and associations between forms and meanings that contribute to its perceived iconicity (e.g., Vinson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A word without an established meaning can indeed seem meaningful, (possibly) because people draw on patterns already present in familiar vocabulary, including contextual cues (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Snefjella et al., 2020)</ref> and associations between forms and meanings that contribute to its perceived iconicity (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Vinson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we focus on the latter aspect and develop the idea that (sub)lexical patterns associated with iconicity in familiar vocabulary may help constrain the meanings people construct for unfamiliar, novel words.

Pseudo-(or novel) words (i.e., readable strings of letters that follow the orthographic and phonological regularities of a language while lacking an established lexical entry) offer a particularly informative way to investigate this process (Marson et al., 2026; Martínez-Tomás et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Pseudo-(or novel) words (i.e., readable strings of letters that follow the orthographic and phonological regularities of a language while lacking an established lexical entry) offer a particularly informative way to investigate this process <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Marson et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Martínez-Tomás et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Previous studies have shown that these stimuli activate semantic information during implicit processing (Gatti et al., 2023), elicit systematic affective judgments (Gatti, Raveling, et al., 2024; Loulidi-Fernández et al., under review; van Eijkelenburg et al., 2026; see also Joosse et al., 2025, for related evidence from fictional characters' names; and Gatti et al., in press, for related evidence on spatial judgments), and support explicit choices about meaning (Bonandrini et al., 2026; Gatti, Rodio, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown that these stimuli activate semantic information during implicit processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Gatti et al., 2023)</ref>, elicit systematic affective judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Gatti, Raveling, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Loulidi-Fernández et al., under review;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">van Eijkelenburg et al., 2026</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Joosse et al., 2025, for</ref> related evidence from fictional characters' names; and <ref type="bibr">Gatti et al., in press</ref>, for related evidence on spatial judgments), and support explicit choices about meaning <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bonandrini et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Gatti, Rodio, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: More directly, de Varda et al. (2024) demonstrated that people generate definitions whose semantic representations are more closely aligned with the intended pseudoword than with other items (see also Martínez-Tomás et al., 2026; Stagnitto et al., 2027).
text.formatted: More directly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">de Varda et al. (2024)</ref> demonstrated that people generate definitions whose semantic representations are more closely aligned with the intended pseudoword than with other items (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Martínez-Tomás et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Stagnitto et al., 2027)</ref>.

text.text: The question emerging from this evidence thus concerns what makes a particular form more compatible with the interpretation that a speaker constructs, and which properties of familiar vocabulary can (eventually) explain this variation.
An unfamiliar string can recruit knowledge acquired through the words that a speaker already knows.

The Complementary Learning Systems, for example, highlights that the neocortex taps into existing conceptual knowledge, using it as a structural foundation to generate new meanings (Davis & Gaskell, 2009; McClelland et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The Complementary Learning Systems, for example, highlights that the neocortex taps into existing conceptual knowledge, using it as a structural foundation to generate new meanings <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Davis & Gaskell, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">McClelland et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This previously stored knowledge can be accessed through different pathways, including lexical resemblance (i.e., coactivation of lexical neighbors; Bailey & Hahn, 2001) and recurring associations between subword units and semantic features (i.e., iconicity; Sidhu, 2025).
text.formatted: This previously stored knowledge can be accessed through different pathways, including lexical resemblance (i.e., coactivation of lexical neighbors; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bailey & Hahn, 2001)</ref> and recurring associations between subword units and semantic features (i.e., iconicity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Sidhu, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For example, English phonaesthemes such as gl-, occurring in words related to light and vision, illustrate how repeated correspondences acquire psychological relevance even outside compositional morphology (e.g., Bergen, 2004), and, more broadly, form-meaning mappings contain statistical regularities distributed across the vocabulary (Monaghan et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For example, English phonaesthemes such as gl-, occurring in words related to light and vision, illustrate how repeated correspondences acquire psychological relevance even outside compositional morphology (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bergen, 2004)</ref>, and, more broadly, form-meaning mappings contain statistical regularities distributed across the vocabulary <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Monaghan et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Within this context, distributional semantic models provide a computational account of how linguistic experience can support such generalization by learning representations from patterns of contextual usage (Günther et al., 2019), and models incorporating subword information, such as fastText, also construct representations for unfamiliar strings from the distributional histories of their constituent character sequences (Bojanowski et al., 2017), making it possible to connect familiar lexical knowledge with the semantic information evoked by unfamiliar forms.
text.formatted: Within this context, distributional semantic models provide a computational account of how linguistic experience can support such generalization by learning representations from patterns of contextual usage <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Günther et al., 2019)</ref>, and models incorporating subword information, such as fastText, also construct representations for unfamiliar strings from the distributional histories of their constituent character sequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bojanowski et al., 2017)</ref>, making it possible to connect familiar lexical knowledge with the semantic information evoked by unfamiliar forms.

text.text: Within this account of form-meaning mapping, it is crucial to distinguish iconicity -the perceived resemblance between aspects of a linguistic form and its meaning -from systematicity -statistical correspondences between forms and semantic or functional properties (Dingemanse, 2012; Dingemanse et al., 2015; Emmorey, 2014; Winter et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Within this account of form-meaning mapping, it is crucial to distinguish iconicity -the perceived resemblance between aspects of a linguistic form and its meaning -from systematicity -statistical correspondences between forms and semantic or functional properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dingemanse, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Dingemanse et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Emmorey, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Winter et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These properties can overlap (McLean & Motamedi, 2026), but recurring associations can guide interpretation through learned correspondences based on statistical co-occurrence of sublexical features in language use (Dingemanse et al., 2015; Winter & Perlman, 2021), whereas iconicity additionally concerns the experience that a form resembles what it conveys (Dingemanse et al., 2020; Occhino et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These properties can overlap <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(McLean & Motamedi, 2026)</ref>, but recurring associations can guide interpretation through learned correspondences based on statistical co-occurrence of sublexical features in language use <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dingemanse et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Winter & Perlman, 2021)</ref>, whereas iconicity additionally concerns the experience that a form resembles what it conveys <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dingemanse et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Occhino et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Research across spoken and signed languages has established iconicity as a pervasive dimension of linguistic organization (de Varda & Marelli, 2025; Perniss et al., 2010; Perniss & Vigliocco, 2014), with graded variation across familiar vocabulary (Perry et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Research across spoken and signed languages has established iconicity as a pervasive dimension of linguistic organization <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(de Varda & Marelli, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Perniss et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Perniss & Vigliocco, 2014)</ref>, with graded variation across familiar vocabulary <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Perry et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Its cognitive relevance includes proposed contributions to identifying referents and establishing new lexical representations (Imai & Kita, 2014), supported by several possible perceptual, associative, and linguistic mechanisms (Sidhu & Pexman, 2018a).
text.formatted: Its cognitive relevance includes proposed contributions to identifying referents and establishing new lexical representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Imai & Kita, 2014)</ref>, supported by several possible perceptual, associative, and linguistic mechanisms <ref type="bibr">(Sidhu & Pexman, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, iconicity is patterned by semantics: words referring to sensory experiences, particularly sound and touch, tend to receive higher iconicity ratings (Hinojosa et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2017), while semantic neighborhood structure also relates to perceived iconicity (Sidhu & Pexman, 2018b).
text.formatted: Crucially, iconicity is patterned by semantics: words referring to sensory experiences, particularly sound and touch, tend to receive higher iconicity ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hinojosa et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Winter et al., 2017)</ref>, while semantic neighborhood structure also relates to perceived iconicity <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Sidhu & Pexman, 2018b)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, high iconic words tend to refer to specific entities and are also characterized by higher degrees of abstractness, and emotionality (Calvillo-Torres et al., 2025; de Varda et al., 2025; de Zubicaray & Hinojosa, 2026; Hinojosa et al., 2026; Sidhu, 2027; Winter et al., 2024). Thompson et al. (2020) directly connected these observations to distributional semantics, showing that semantic vectors predict iconicity ratings for English words and American Sign Language signs.

(2020)</ref> directly connected these observations to distributional semantics, showing that semantic vectors predict iconicity ratings for English words and American Sign Language signs.

text.text: Thus, current data indicates that the organization of familiar vocabulary contains information about which meaning patterns are associated with perceived form-meaning resemblance.
Furthermore, iconic words tend to be more widely known despite appearing less frequently in everyday speech (Sidhu, 2027).
text.formatted: Furthermore, iconic words tend to be more widely known despite appearing less frequently in everyday speech <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Sidhu, 2027)</ref>.

text.text: Based on this evidence, here we extend the prediction of iconicity in familiar vocabulary to the interpretation of unfamiliar forms, asking whether information learned from human resemblance judgments predicts the semantic quality and specificity of pseudoword definitions.
Testing this proposal requires distinguishing the production of a possible meaning from its semantic fit, operationalized here in terms of quality and specificity.

Semantic quality concerns how closely a definition aligns with the model-derived semantic information associated with its target form, consistent with computational approaches to representing pseudoword semantics and evaluating human-generated definitions (e.g., Chuang et al., 2021; de Varda et al., 2024), while specificity, by contrast, concerns how selectively a definition fits its intended target relative to alternative forms, reflecting the broader distinction between semantic compatibility and informativeness in context (Frank & Goodman, 2012; Degen, 2023).
text.formatted: Semantic quality concerns how closely a definition aligns with the model-derived semantic information associated with its target form, consistent with computational approaches to representing pseudoword semantics and evaluating human-generated definitions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chuang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">de Varda et al., 2024)</ref>, while specificity, by contrast, concerns how selectively a definition fits its intended target relative to alternative forms, reflecting the broader distinction between semantic compatibility and informativeness in context <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Frank & Goodman, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Degen, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A definition may therefore express a broadly plausible concept while providing relatively little information that distinguishes its intended pseudoword from others, paralleling the distinction between descriptively accurate and discriminative representations (Cohn-Gordon et al., 2018; de Varda et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A definition may therefore express a broadly plausible concept while providing relatively little information that distinguishes its intended pseudoword from others, paralleling the distinction between descriptively accurate and discriminative representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cohn-Gordon et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">de Varda et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these outcomes distinguish alignment with an interpretation from the relative selectivity of that alignment.

In the present study (see Figure 1 for an overview of the study), we addressed this question by learning mappings from familiar-word representations to human iconicity ratings and applying them to pseudowords, building on approaches that extrapolate lexical judgments from embeddings (Hollis et al., 2017) and transfer learned lexical properties to unfamiliar strings (Gatti & Günther, 2026).
text.formatted: In the present study (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for an overview of the study), we addressed this question by learning mappings from familiar-word representations to human iconicity ratings and applying them to pseudowords, building on approaches that extrapolate lexical judgments from embeddings <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Hollis et al., 2017)</ref> and transfer learned lexical properties to unfamiliar strings <ref type="bibr">(Gatti & Günther, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Reanalyzing existing data, we compared letter counts, adjacent bigrams, open bigrams, and fastText embeddings, using 14,750 iconicity-rated English words and 9,560 definitions for 899 pseudowords, and we then computationally indexed pseudoword-definition semantic quality and specificity.

If iconicity-related lexical information contributes to novel interpretation, higher predicted iconicity should accompany greater semantic quality and specificity, with the representational comparisons identifying which recoverable information supports this relationship. regression models and predictive performance was evaluated through nested crossvalidation, and models were subsequently refitted on all familiar words and applied to 899 pseudowords without retraining (A).

Definition quality was computed as the cosine similarity between each pseudoword and its human-generated definition, whereas definition specificity was calculated by subtracting the mean similarity between that definition and alternative pseudowords from the same collection from its similarity with the target (B).
Associations between predicted iconicity and pseudoword-level definition quality and specificity were assessed using collection-adjusted Spearman correlations (C).
Iconicity ratings were retrieved from the English norms collected by Winter et al. (2024).
text.formatted: Iconicity ratings were retrieved from the English norms collected by <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Winter et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: This dataset contains ratings for 14,776 words, based on 161,057 judgments collected from 1,419 American English speakers.
Participants evaluated the perceived resemblance between a word's sound and its meaning on a seven-point scale, ranging from 1 (not iconic at all) to 7 (very iconic).
Each word received at least ten valid judgments.
These ratings therefore provide an item-level estimate of the extent to which speakers perceive a word's form as resembling its referent or meaning.
For the present analyses, word forms were normalized to lowercase and restricted to alphabetic, single-word entries.
The resulting dataset comprised 14,750 distinct words.
Mean iconicity ratings served as the dependent variable in the ridge regression analyses described below.
Pseudowords and their definitions were obtained from the two English datasets investigated by de Varda et al. (2024).
text.formatted: Pseudowords and their definitions were obtained from the two English datasets investigated by de <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Varda et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: The first collection contained definitions for 499 pseudowords originally investigated by Gatti, Raveling, et al. (2024) in which the stimuli had been generated using Wuggy (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010), with its English orthographic module and constraints on subsyllabic structure, letter length, and transition frequencies.
text.formatted: The first collection contained definitions for 499 pseudowords originally investigated by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Gatti, Raveling, et al. (2024)</ref> in which the stimuli had been generated using Wuggy <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010)</ref>, with its English orthographic module and constraints on subsyllabic structure, letter length, and transition frequencies.

text.text: Participants were presented with sets of six pseudowords and selected the items that elicited the most positive and most negative emotional responses; they subsequently provided a plausible definition for each selected item using an affirmative sentence.

The second collection contained a different set of 400 pseudowords from the same original set of 1,500 items (i.e., these items were selected from the original stimulus pool after excluding the 499 pseudowords included in the first collection).
Participants defined each item using a short affirmative sentence and were instructed to provide a plausible interpretation when the item was unfamiliar.
We applied the published response-quality exclusions to the two collections, removing 74 pseudoword responses.
Before embedding extraction, occurrences of the target pseudoword were removed from its definition using case-insensitive whole-token matching.
Whitespace was subsequently normalized, and one response that became empty was excluded.
This procedure retained 5,609 definitions for the first collection and 3,951 for the second, for a total of 9,560 definitions.
Since the two stimulus sets did not overlap, we pooled their 899 pseudowords and all subsequent association analyses were conducted at the pseudoword level.

To quantify the information available in orthographic form, we constructed three separate representations: letter counts, adjacent bigram counts, and open bigram counts with identical procedures and feature inventories for existing words and pseudowords.

The letter representation consisted of 26 dimensions corresponding to the letters of the English alphabet, where each dimension encoded the number of occurrences of the corresponding letter in the string.
Thus, repeated letters contributed their full counts, and the representation did not encode letter position.
For adjacent bigrams, we first added distinct beginning-and end-of-word markers to each string and then counted every pair of consecutive elements.
For example, cat was represented by the pairs #c, ca, at, and t#.
The inventory comprised 728 possible features: 676 letter-letter combinations, 26 beginning-marker-letter combinations, and 26 letter-end-marker combinations.
Of these, 552 occurred in the existing-word training data.
Open bigrams encoded ordered pairs of elements occurring anywhere within the boundary-marked string.
This representation therefore included adjacent pairs as well as nonadjacent pairs, while preserving their relative order.
For example, cat additionally contributed the pair ct.
Boundary-letter pairs were included, whereas the pair consisting only of the beginning and end markers was excluded.
The inventory again contained 728 possible features, of which 710 occurred in the training data.
The main embedding model used for the main analyses was fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The main embedding model used for the main analyses was fastText <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bojanowski et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Distributional semantic models (DSMs) learn semantic representations from regularities in the linguistic contexts in which words occur, so that words appearing in similar contexts receive similar representations.
FastText takes subword information into account by learning vectors for the character n-grams associated with each word, in addition to a vector for the complete lexical item.
This solution improves the representation of infrequent words and also allows semantic vectors to be retrieved for strings of letters that are absent from the model's vocabulary.
Novel words can therefore be represented by relying on the distributional information associated with their constituent n-grams.
The model used here was trained on English Wikipedia using the skip-gram method, with 300 dimensions, character n-grams of three to six characters, and a context window of five words.
As an example, consider the word houses, composed of several three-to six-character n-grams.
Its fastText representation is obtained by summing the whole-word vector and the vectors of its constituent ngrams, and then dividing by the number of vectors included in the sum.
These include, for example, the trigrams <ho, hou, ous, and es>, the four-grams <hou, hous, and ses>, the five-grams <hous and ouses, and the six-grams <house and houses.
text.formatted: These include, for example, the trigrams <ho, hou, ous, and es>, the four-grams <hou, hous, and ses>, the five-grams <hous and ouses, and the six-grams <house and houses.

text.text: Beginning-and end-of-word markers (< and >) are encoded as characters, so that <ho and es>, for example, count as trigrams.
text.formatted: Beginning-and end-of-word markers (< and >) are encoded as characters, so that <ho and es>, for example, count as trigrams.

text.text: A similar approach can be applied to unattested strings to capture the semantic information associated with novel words.
Let's take as an example the string quocky, which is absent from the model's vocabulary.
In this case, its representation is obtained by averaging only the vectors of its constituent n-grams, including, for example, the trigrams <qu, quo, uoc, ock, cky, and ky>.
text.formatted: In this case, its representation is obtained by averaging only the vectors of its constituent n-grams, including, for example, the trigrams <qu, quo, uoc, ock, cky, and ky>.

text.text: Thus, even without a whole-word vector for quocky, the model can extract information learned from its subword units in natural language.
Using fastText, we therefore obtained 300-dimensional representations for all words and pseudowords included in the analyses.
Definitions were represented by averaging the native fastText vectors of their constituent content tokens.
Specifically, definitions were normalized to Unicode NFC, converted to lowercase, and tokenized into sequences of letters, allowing internal apostrophes.
Punctuation separated tokens, and numerical strings were discarded.
We removed the 175 English stopwords in the Snowball list (https://snowballstem.org/algorithms/english/stop.txt) and computed the unweighted arithmetic mean of the remaining token vectors.
text.formatted: We removed the 175 English stopwords in the Snowball list (<ref type="url" target="https://snowballstem.org/algorithms/english/stop.txt">https://snowballstem.org/algorithms/english/stop.txt</ref>) and computed the unweighted arithmetic mean of the remaining token vectors.

text.text: Repeated tokens were retained and contributed repeatedly to this mean.
Token vectors were averaged before normalization and then the resulting definition vector was normalized when computing cosine similarity.
Three definitions contained no tokens after stopword removal and were excluded from the fastText outcome calculations.
The remaining 9,557 definitions provided valid scores for all 899 pseudowords.

The decision to use fastText as the main embedding model was further supported by Chen et al. (2026), who compared five large language models with fastText and human performance in the two experiments performed by Gatti, Rodio, et al. (2024) and showed that fastText more closely reproduced human choices when the response alternatives were pseudowords.

(2026)</ref>, who compared five large language models with fastText and human performance in the two experiments performed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Gatti, Rodio, et al. (2024)</ref> and showed that fastText more closely reproduced human choices when the response alternatives were pseudowords.

text.text: To assess whether the results depended on the particular representation used to predict iconicity or evaluate definitions, we additionally considered ten pretrained transformer encoders; these models produce fixed-length embeddings suitable for comparing texts through vector similarity (see Table 1).
text.formatted: To assess whether the results depended on the particular representation used to predict iconicity or evaluate definitions, we additionally considered ten pretrained transformer encoders; these models produce fixed-length embeddings suitable for comparing texts through vector similarity (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Their sentence-level training objectives encourage semantically related texts to receive similar representations, extending the sentence-embedding approach described by Reimers and Gurevych (2019).
text.formatted: Their sentence-level training objectives encourage semantically related texts to receive similar representations, extending the sentence-embedding approach described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Reimers and Gurevych (2019)</ref>.

text.text: The model set included BERT-based encoders, a RoBERTa-based sentence encoder, the multilingual XLM-R-based BGE-M3 model, MPNet, and MiniLM.
These models differ in their pretrained representations, sentence-embedding training, dimensionality, and aggregation procedures.

For example, GIST uses guided selection of contrastive training examples (Solatorio, 2024), whereas supervised SimCSE learns sentence representations using entailment and contradiction relations (Gao et al., 2021).

text.text: We retained these differences as alternative operationalizations of semantic information.

GIST-large (Solatorio, 2024); GTE-large (Li et al., 2023); MiniLM (Wang et al., 2020); Mixedbread Embed Large (Lee et al., 2024); MPNet (Song et al., 2020); SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019); and SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021).

text.text: MiniLM and MPNet were used in their sentence-transformers variants linked in the table.
Unlike fastText, these encoders construct representations through bidirectional interactions among the tokens in an input sequence.
For a definition, each token's representation is influenced by the surrounding tokens, allowing the final embedding to incorporate contextual and compositional information.
The sequence is then reduced to a single vector using the aggregation procedure specified for that model.
Isolated words were submitted as individual input sequences, without a carrier sentence.
A word could therefore be represented by one or several subword tokens, together with the model's native special tokens.
Pseudowords were processed in exactly the same way.

Their representations were constructed from the subword units identified by the tokenizer and the interactions among those units, rather than requiring a vocabulary entry for the complete (pseudo)word.
Definitions were submitted as complete cleaned sequences, retaining stopwords, punctuation, and original case before modelspecific tokenization.
Embeddings were retrieved through the Transformers Python library (Wolf et al., 2020) using fixed pretrained checkpoints.
text.formatted: Embeddings were retrieved through the Transformers Python library <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Wolf et al., 2020)</ref> using fixed pretrained checkpoints.

text.text: Models were evaluated without gradient updates or adaptation to the iconicity ratings or definition data.
For mean aggregation, padding positions were excluded using the attention mask, while native special tokens were retained.
For CLS aggregation, we extracted the final hidden representation of the initial classification token.
For supervised SimCSE, we retained the model's native pooler transformation.
E5 inputs received the prefix "query: " for all three input types; the remaining models received no additional prefix.
All encoder embeddings were normalized to unit length and no inputs were truncated.
The same checkpoint, tokenizer, prefix, and aggregation procedure were used for existing words, pseudowords, and definitions within each model.
The ten encoders used the same set of 9,560 definitions.

To estimate the iconicity information captured by each representation, we used representational content analysis (RCA; a term proposed by Hussain et al., 2024, but note that the use of embeddings to extrapolate psychologically interpretable judgments predates the RCA label, Hollis et al., 2017).
text.formatted: To estimate the iconicity information captured by each representation, we used representational content analysis (RCA; a term proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Hussain et al., 2024</ref>, but note that the use of embeddings to extrapolate psychologically interpretable judgments predates the RCA label, <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Hollis et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: RCA tests whether a psychologically relevant property is recoverable from the dimensions of a representational space: a mapping is learned between these dimensions and independently measured behavioral judgments, and its predictive performance is evaluated on held-out items.

Here, we learned a (ridge) linear mapping from existing-word representations to human iconicity ratings and then applied it to pseudowords represented in the same space, following the approach used by Gatti and Günther (2026) to predict pseudoword memorability.
text.formatted: Here, we learned a (ridge) linear mapping from existing-word representations to human iconicity ratings and then applied it to pseudowords represented in the same space, following the approach used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Gatti and Günther (2026)</ref> to predict pseudoword memorability.

text.text: For the semantic models, the resulting predictions therefore index the component of iconicity that is predictable from semantic information.

We first fitted four separate ridge regressions predicting mean human iconicity ratings for the 14,750 existing words from letter counts, adjacent bigram counts, open bigram counts, or the 300 fastText dimensions.
Ridge regression applies an L2 penalty to the regression coefficients, allowing correlated and numerous predictors to be included while limiting overfitting.
Models were fitted using the glmnet package in R (Friedman et al., 2010), with the mixing parameter set to α = 0, an intercept, and predictor standardization within the training data.
text.formatted: Models were fitted using the glmnet package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Friedman et al., 2010)</ref>, with the mixing parameter set to α = 0, an intercept, and predictor standardization within the training data.

text.text: Predictive performance was assessed using nested cross-validation: the words were divided into five outer folds, with each fold serving once as the held-out test set.
Within each outer training set, tenfold cross-validation selected the penalty from 100 logarithmically spaced values between 10 4 and 10 -4 .
We selected the penalty minimizing cross-validated mean squared error.
Performance was calculated from the concatenated outer-fold predictions, ensuring that each word was evaluated using a model trained without that word.
We report Spearman correlations between predicted and observed ratings, root mean squared error, and predictive R² , calculated as 𝑅 !
= 1 -""# ""$ , where SSE is the sum of squared prediction errors and SST is the total sum of squared deviations from the observed grand mean.
For prediction of pseudoword iconicity, each model was subsequently fitted to all 14,750 existing words, with the penalty selected through ten-fold cross-validation.
The fitted mapping was then applied to the corresponding features of the 899 pseudowords.
Overall, these predicted iconicities index the iconicity information recoverable from a given set of features in the representations included.
Firstly, we quantified definition quality as the cosine similarity between the representation of a pseudoword and the representation of a definition provided for that pseudoword.
Cosine similarity is the most widely used measure of semantic similarity in distributional semantic models (Günther et al., 2019; Turney & Pantel, 2010).
text.formatted: Cosine similarity is the most widely used measure of semantic similarity in distributional semantic models <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Günther et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Turney & Pantel, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: It is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their Euclidean norms, and therefore compares their directions independently of their magnitudes:
Here, 𝐩 % denotes the vector for pseudoword 𝑖, and 𝐝 %& denotes the vector for its 𝑗th definition.
text.formatted: Here, 𝐩 % denotes the vector for pseudoword 𝑖, and 𝐝 %& denotes the vector for its 𝑗th definition.

text.text: Higher values indicate stronger alignment between the semantic information associated with the pseudoword and the content expressed in the definition; this measure therefore operationalizes definition quality as semantic correspondence.
We calculated the score separately for each definition and then averaged these scores within pseudoword.
Then, we assessed whether a definition was particularly aligned with its intended pseudoword relative to other pseudowords.
For each definition, specificity was calculated by subtracting its mean cosine similarity with all other pseudowords from the same original collection from its similarity with the intended target:
Here, 𝐶 ' denotes the set of pseudowords in collection 𝑠, and 𝑁 ' is the number of pseudowords in that collection.
The comparison therefore involved 498 alternative pseudowords for the first collection and 399 for the second.

Higher specificity indicates that a definition is more closely associated with its intended pseudoword than with the alternatives available in that collection; this measure thus indexes target discrimination.
As for quality, specificity was calculated separately for each definition and subsequently averaged within pseudoword.
Then we performed the main analyses, which related the four predicted iconicity scores to fastTextbased definition quality and specificity.
Because the two collections differed in their designs, associations were adjusted for collection membership.
Predictor and outcome scores were first converted to ranks across all 899 pseudowords, using average ranks for ties.
We then removed collection-specific means from the ranks and correlated the resulting residuals.
The resulting coefficients are collection-adjusted Spearman correlations.
Two-sided significance tests used 4,999 permutations of pseudoword predictor scores within collection.
The same permutations were used across representations, and p-values were calculated with a +1 correction, yielding a minimum attainable p value of .0002.
Unadjusted 95% confidence intervals were obtained from 2,000 bootstrap samples of pseudowords, stratified by collection, with ranks recomputed in each sample.
The four predictors and two metrics yielded eight main tests, to which we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) to control the false discovery rate.
text.formatted: The four predictors and two metrics yielded eight main tests, to which we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref> to control the false discovery rate.

text.text: We report the resulting adjusted p values, labeled as q, alongside raw p values.

Finally, to evaluate whether the association depended on using fastText both to predict iconicity and to score definitions, we repeated the iconicity-training procedure separately for each of the ten transformer encoders.

Each ridge model used only that encoder's vector dimensions and was trained on the same 14,750 words, using the same outer folds, inner folds, penalty grid, and selection criterion as the main models.
We then predicted iconicity for the same 899 pseudowords.
First, the ten encoder-based iconicity predictions were correlated with the fastText quality and specificity scores.
These 20 tests changed the representation used to predict iconicity while holding the definition metric constant.
Second, we crossed all eleven vector-based iconicity predictors (i.e., fastText and the ten encoders) with quality and specificity scores computed using each of the eleven representations.
This produced two directional 11 × 11 matrices, one for each outcome.
All robustness analyses used the same collection-adjusted correlations, permutation procedure, and bootstrap procedure as the main analyses.
These robustness tests are reported with raw p values.
All four feature sets predicted iconicity ratings in held-out words (Figure 2).
text.formatted: All four feature sets predicted iconicity ratings in held-out words (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The letter model achieved a predictive R² of .135, with a Spearman correlation of .353 between predicted and observed ratings and an RMSE of .832.
Adjacent bigrams achieved R² = .210, ρ = .423, and RMSE = .795, whereas open bigrams achieved R² = .171, ρ = .385, and RMSE = .815.
The fastText model had the highest predictive performance among the four main models, with R² = .315, ρ = .515, and RMSE = .741.
Thus, a linear mapping from the fastText dimensions accounted for approximately 31.5% of the variance in iconicity ratings under held-out evaluation.
Representational content analysis of iconicity ratings for 14,750 English words using letters, adjacent bigrams, open bigrams, and fastText dimensions.
We next examined whether the iconicity predictions generalized to differences in the definitions provided for pseudowords (Figure 3).
text.formatted: We next examined whether the iconicity predictions generalized to differences in the definitions provided for pseudowords (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: FastText-based predicted iconicity was positively associated with definition quality, ρ = .175, 95% CI [.111, .234], p = .0002, q = .0008.
Pseudowords receiving higher predicted iconicity scores therefore elicited definitions that were more closely aligned with their fastText representations.

A comparable association was observed for definition specificity, ρ = .174, 95% CI [.108, .236], p = .0002, q = .0008, where higher predicted iconicity was associated with definitions that distinguished their intended pseudoword more strongly from other pseudowords in the same collection.
The three orthographic predictors showed associations close to zero for both outcomes.
None was significant after correction, with all six q values equal to .9970.
These results indicate that the component of iconicity recovered from fastText representations was associated with both the semantic alignment and target specificity of pseudoword definitions 1.
Although orthographic features predicted iconicity ratings for existing words, their resulting pseudoword predictions showed no association with either definition measure.
Each encoder supported prediction of existing-word iconicity under nested cross-validation (Figure 4A).

text.text: Predictive R² ranged from .315 for MiniLM-L12 to .391 for E5-large-v2.

Spearman correlations between fastText-predicted iconicity and these new measures were negligible for both definition quality (ρ = .008, p = .804) and specificity (ρ = -.005, p = .886) and were significantly smaller than those obtained using the pseudoword vectors (p < .001).

text.text: Thus, these results argue against the explanation that the original associations simply reflect the trivial activation of the closest orthographically similar familiar words.
The positive associations therefore generalized to iconicity predictions derived from several representations other than fastText.
Their magnitudes varied across encoders, and stronger prediction of existing-word iconicity did not necessarily correspond to a stronger association with pseudoword definition scores.
For example, E5-large-v2 achieved the highest word-prediction R² , whereas SimCSE BERT-large showed the strongest associations with the fastText outcomes among the ten encoders.

To focus on associations that could not arise solely from using exactly the same representation in both stages, we examined the off-diagonal cells separately.
All 110 off-diagonal quality correlations were positive, and 92 were significant with p < .05.

text.text: For specificity, 108 of the 110 off-diagonal correlations were positive, and 82 were significant.
Off-diagonal correlations ranged from .005 to .320 for quality and from -.010 to .317 for specificity.
The association between semantically predictable iconicity and definition scores therefore extended across different representations used for iconicity prediction and definition evaluation.
This pattern indicates that the results were not confined to the reuse of fastText in both stages.
At the same time, the variation in effect sizes shows that the strength of the association depended on how semantic information was represented and measured.
In the present study, we investigated whether iconicity-related information learned from familiar vocabulary is associated with the meanings people construct for unfamiliar forms.
Across 899 pseudowords, higher fastText-derived iconicity predictions accompanied definitions with greater semantic quality and specificity.

Notably, by transferring a mapping learned from familiar-word resemblance judgments to unfamiliar forms, these findings connect the semantic organization of perceived iconicity with variation in novel meaning construction.
Theoretically, this pattern favors a continuous account of lexical knowledge in which learned formmeaning relations remain productive beyond the particular items through which they were acquired.

Discriminative theories formalize this possibility as mappings between sublexical cues and distributed semantic information (Baayen et al., 2019), with such mappings also predicting aspects of pseudoword comprehension and production (Chuang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Discriminative theories formalize this possibility as mappings between sublexical cues and distributed semantic information <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baayen et al., 2019)</ref>, with such mappings also predicting aspects of pseudoword comprehension and production <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chuang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Within this perspective, a novel form elicits a semantic response through previously learned relations.

Our findings complement this framework by identifying iconicity-related structure as a dimension along which familiar-word knowledge generalizes to explicit interpretation, extending evidence from semantic priming, affective judgments, and meaning selection (Gatti et al., 2023; Gatti, Raveling, et al., 2024; Gatti, Rodio, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Our findings complement this framework by identifying iconicity-related structure as a dimension along which familiar-word knowledge generalizes to explicit interpretation, extending evidence from semantic priming, affective judgments, and meaning selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Gatti et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Gatti, Raveling, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Gatti, Rodio, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, this extension connects two processes that are often considered separately: the perception of motivated relationships between form and meaning, and the use of accumulated lexical knowledge to interpret a form that has no established meaning.

Crucially, the fact that fastTextderived iconicity predictions, but not predictions based on letter or bigram information alone, were associated with the semantic properties of pseudoword definitions suggests that the information relevant to novel meaning construction cannot be reduced to formal resemblance.
Rather, it may depend on the relationships between sublexical patterns and the meanings with which they have become associated throughout linguistic experience.
In this sense, iconicity-related information may provide a particularly informative dimension through which previously acquired lexical knowledge generalizes to unfamiliar forms.

The present results suggest that these processes may be related insofar as the regularities associated with iconicity in familiar words provide information relevant to constructing meanings for pseudowords.

This account does not require unfamiliar forms to possess an intrinsically "correct" meaning, but instead, their interpretation may reflect the extent to which their properties are compatible with semantic patterns established through linguistic experience cosnistesnt with prior research showing that several sematic factors contribute to iconicity (such as the tendency to depict specific references, or to show higher degrees of abstractness, emotionality or sensory referents; Calvillo-Torres et al., 2025; de Varda et al., 2025; Sidhu, 2027; Winter et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This account does not require unfamiliar forms to possess an intrinsically "correct" meaning, but instead, their interpretation may reflect the extent to which their properties are compatible with semantic patterns established through linguistic experience cosnistesnt with prior research showing that several sematic factors contribute to iconicity (such as the tendency to depict specific references, or to show higher degrees of abstractness, emotionality or sensory referents; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Calvillo-Torres et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">de Varda et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Sidhu, 2027;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Winter et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The specificity result gives this account particular theoretical weight because it concerns the selectivity of a form-meaning relationship.
Higher embedding-derived iconicity predictions accompanied definitions that aligned more strongly with their intended pseudoword relative to competing forms.

This pattern motivates an account of interpretation as graded activation among semantic possibilities, consistent with models in which distributed meaning representations compete during word recognition (Rodd et al., 2004).
text.formatted: This pattern motivates an account of interpretation as graded activation among semantic possibilities, consistent with models in which distributed meaning representations compete during word recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Rodd et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: That is, prior linguistic experience supplies different degrees of support for candidate interpretations, making some meanings more compatible with a particular form than others.

The semantic structure associated with iconicity can therefore be conceived as a source of probabilistic constraints on meaning construction, organizing candidate interpretations while allowing individual knowledge and context to influence the interpretation ultimately expressed.

Importantly, the association with specificity suggests that iconicity-related information may do more than facilitate the generation of broadly plausible meanings: it may also contribute to distinguishing among alternative interpretations, increasing the extent to which a definition captures the semantic properties associated with a particular novel form.
This proposal also connects the semantic patterning of iconicity with the complementary functions of resemblance and arbitrariness in language.

Iconicity varies systematically across semantic regions, including sensory meanings (Thompson et al., 2020; Winter et al., 2017), whereas arbitrary forms can support abstraction beyond specific sensory depictions (Lupyan & Winter, 2018).
text.formatted: Iconicity varies systematically across semantic regions, including sensory meanings <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Thompson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Winter et al., 2017)</ref>, whereas arbitrary forms can support abstraction beyond specific sensory depictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Lupyan & Winter, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Within this broader division, iconicity-related regularities offer resources for selecting and differentiating interpretations, alongside the categorical flexibility supported by conventional lexical knowledge.

Our results locate this relationship at the productive interface between familiar vocabulary and unfamiliar forms, connecting the organization of iconic meanings with the construction of new semantic associations (Dingemanse et al., 2015; Winter et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Our results locate this relationship at the productive interface between familiar vocabulary and unfamiliar forms, connecting the organization of iconic meanings with the construction of new semantic associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Dingemanse et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Winter et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings also contribute to theories of iconicity by demonstrating that iconic resemblance and distributional generalization are complementary cognitive mechanisms, rather than competing ones.
Rather than viewing iconicity as a direct replication of external reality, our data can be interpreted in light of proposals like the analogue-building model (Emmorey, 2014).
text.formatted: Rather than viewing iconicity as a direct replication of external reality, our data can be interpreted in light of proposals like the analogue-building model <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Emmorey, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This account suggests that linguistic iconicity relies on structured cognitive mapping between schematic representations of multimodal experiences (i.e., perceptual, motor and affective), and semantic representations (Emmorey, 2014; Hinojosa et al., 2027).
text.formatted: This account suggests that linguistic iconicity relies on structured cognitive mapping between schematic representations of multimodal experiences (i.e., perceptual, motor and affective), and semantic representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Emmorey, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Hinojosa et al., 2027)</ref>.

text.text: Our data extend this view by highlighting the role of statistical linguistic experience.

Specifically, we propose that familiar lexical patterns act as scaffolds that organize and facilitate access to resemblance-related semantic information when individuals interpret novel or unfamiliar labels (Perniss et al., 2010; Sidhu & Pexman, 2018a).
text.formatted: Specifically, we propose that familiar lexical patterns act as scaffolds that organize and facilitate access to resemblance-related semantic information when individuals interpret novel or unfamiliar labels <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Perniss et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sidhu & Pexman, 2018a)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, interpreting a novel form may involve more than detecting a resemblance between its physical properties and a potential referent, as it may also involve drawing on previously acquired regularities that link similar forms to related semantic representations.

Consistent with this idea, we suggest that the relationship between form and meaning may be shaped both by the perceptual and experiential correspondences that make certain forms seem motivated and by the distributional structure through which those correspondences become established and available for generalization.

These components need not be mutually exclusive: experiential correspondences may contribute to the emergence of motivated form-meaning relationships, while linguistic experience organizes and reinforces the regularities through which such relationships can be extended to new forms.

By bridging the gap between experiential grounding and learned form-meaning relations, our perspective broadly aligns with theories that link embodied resemblance with the statistical organization of lexical knowledge (Andrews et al., 2014; Louwerse, 2018) and, more specifically, with hybrid accounts of conceptual combination that deal with the processes involved in generating new meaning from old referents (Feldman & Narayanan, 2004; Lynott & Connell, 2010).

text.text: In particular, the crossed-model analyses establish that this association recurs across different representational approaches and architectures, indicating that it can be recovered through several operationalizations of semantic information.
Performance depended on both the task and each representation's role, potentially reflecting differences in how models training organizes semantic similarity.

Training on diverse text pairs, as implemented in E5 and GTE, can support broad semantic coverage, while the selection of informative contrasts can sharpen distinctions between related and unrelated interpretations (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).

text.text: Specifically, predicting iconicity from familiar-word vectors requires relevant information to be recoverable, whereas the pseudoword analyses additionally depend on how unfamiliar forms and definitions are positioned relative to one another.
Generalization to unfamiliar forms therefore provides a complementary criterion for evaluating which aspects of lexical knowledge different representations preserve.
Two further theoretical implications can follow from these findings.
First, the present results suggest a connection between learned lexical regularities and the processes through which lexical invention becomes interpretable in communication.

Accounts of lexical innovation emphasize shared knowledge and the circumstances in which an expression is used (Clark & Clark, 1979), while probabilistic accounts of pragmatic inference explain interpretation through the integration of linguistic information, contextual expectations, and assumptions about informativeness (Frank & Goodman, 2012).
text.formatted: Accounts of lexical innovation emphasize shared knowledge and the circumstances in which an expression is used <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Clark & Clark, 1979)</ref>, while probabilistic accounts of pragmatic inference explain interpretation through the integration of linguistic information, contextual expectations, and assumptions about informativeness <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Frank & Goodman, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that iconicity-related patterns in familiar vocabulary may contribute to this process by making some interpretations of an unfamiliar form more plausible than others.
These graded semantic expectations could provide a starting point for contextual and communicative inference, helping listeners identify what a speaker intends to convey.

This perspective connects spontaneous meaning construction with purposeful lexical invention: in both cases, accumulated lexical knowledge may constrain the interpretations available for a form without an established meaning.
It predicts that compatibility with familiar lexical patterns and communicative context jointly influence the meaning assigned to a novel expression.
Second, the findings connect this account of meaning construction with the proposed role of iconicity in language acquisition.

Iconicity is widespread across spoken and signed vocabularies (Perlman et al., 2018; Perniss et al., 2010), with evidence linking it to semantic aspects of language learning and adult lexical processing (Ortega, 2017; Vinson et al., 2015).

text.text: Adults can also use sound-symbolic information to interpret words from unfamiliar languages (Revill et al., 2014; Van Hoey et al., 2023).

text.text: The present study extends this perspective to the spontaneous construction of meanings for (written) pseudowords.

The pattern observed here, consistent with the idea that adults drawing on learned semantic regularities associated with iconicity to constrain novel meanings, therefore suggests that iconicity-related lexical knowledge remains productive in adulthood and motivates the prediction that these initial interpretive constraints may also facilitate subsequent word learning.
In conclusion, iconicity-related information recovered from familiar-word representations predicts both the semantic alignment and target specificity of human-generated pseudoword definitions.
These findings support a productive view of lexical knowledge, with established vocabulary supplying graded constraints on the construction of unfamiliar meanings.

By connecting human resemblance judgments with the alignment and selectivity of novel definitions, the present study identifies iconicity-related semantic structure as a predictor of novel meaning construction, showing how patterns associated with resemblance in established vocabulary extend to the interpretation of new forms.

text.text: The representational comparison clarifies which iconicity-related information accompanies this variation.
Letter counts and both bigram representations predicted iconicity ratings for held-out existing words, yet their pseudoword predictions showed associations close to zero with definition scores.

FastText-derived predictions, conversely, related to both outcomes supporting an account in which unfamiliar forms acquire interpretive potential through their connections to accumulated (sub)lexical and semantic knowledge.

This contrast is particularly informative because it suggests that the information supporting iconicity judgments for familiar words is not necessarily sufficient to explain how people construct meanings for unfamiliar forms.

Although surface-level orthographic properties may capture some of the formal regularities associated with perceived iconicity, they do not appear to provide the information required to account for the semantic properties of novel definitions.

In the present analyses, associations with definition scores emerged only when formrelated information was represented within a space that also captured distributional relationships across the lexicon.

It should also be noted that form remains (partially) central because fastText constructs pseudoword representations from character n-grams whose vectors are learned through their occurrence in the lexicon (Bojanowski et al., 2017).
text.formatted: It should also be noted that form remains (partially) central because fastText constructs pseudoword representations from character n-grams whose vectors are learned through their occurrence in the lexicon <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bojanowski et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, fastText does not simply discard formal information in favor of meaning; rather, it captures how sublexical patterns are embedded in the lexical environments in which they occur.
The relevant information therefore concerns how sublexical information distribution connect to learned meanings, beyond letter or bigram counts alone.
The control analysis further clarifies this distinction.

Replacing each pseudoword vector with the vector of its closest orthographic neighbor among the model's 20,000 most frequent words yielded negligible associations with definition quality and specificity and these associations were significantly smaller than those obtained with the original pseudoword representations.
The observed relationship therefore cannot readily be explained by the contribution of a single familiar word selected on the basis of orthographic similarity.
Instead, it is consistent with the possibility that the relevant information reflects broader distributional regularities across the lexicon.
A novel form may share sublexical properties with familiar words without simply inheriting the meaning of its closest orthographic neighbor.
This distinction suggests that the interpretive potential of an unfamiliar form may depend on how its features relate to patterns distributed across multiple lexical items.

Although the present analyses do not establish the precise mechanism through which these relationships influence human interpretation, they indicate that orthographic resemblance to a single known word is insufficient to account for the observed associations.
